ar_middle_east_bouldering.blurb: A boulder field on the east side of Horseshoe Canyon Ranch in the Ozarks of north-central Arkansas. This is one of the canyon's quieter corners, so you may have the problems to yourself. The sandstone blocks are scattered through thick brush, and a few lines remain unclimbed projects. The 18 problems here lean hard: two easy V2s, then a run of V5 to V7 lines, and a solid group from V9 up to V13. It suits strong boulderers more than anyone looking for a warm-up circuit, so bring several pads and plan to hunt a little for the blocks.

ar_rosie_s_cantina_area.blurb: A tight cluster of mostly bolted routes at Horseshoe Canyon Ranch in north-central Arkansas, sitting at the right-hand end of the Middle East section. The wall is sandstone and holds 18 lines, 14 of them sport and the rest trad, with a top-rope line or two as well. Difficulty runs from about 5.7 up to the low 5.11s, with the bulk of the climbs between 5.8 and 5.10, so it works for a mixed group that wants a short, varied day away from the busier walls. You reach it by following the Magoo Rock trail from the Middle East boulders.

bc_creek_wall.blurb: A modest wall within Begbie Bluffs, just outside Revelstoke in the Columbia-Shuswap region of British Columbia. Of its 18 routes, 17 are sport and one is trad, though top-rope lines also exist. Grades start near 5.4 and stretch to about 5.12, with most of the climbs between 5.8 and 5.10. That makes it a reasonable pick for a party mixing moderates with a few harder pitches. The far right end of the wall has a handful of bolted lines starting from a deep groove or corner, and the walk in is brief.

ct_sport_routes.blurb: The bolted lines on the Firewall, a small basalt cliff in Southington in central Connecticut on the Metacomet traprock ridge. The wall is only around 70 feet tall and is known for some big roofs. Of the 18 routes, 11 are sport and 7 trad, from the 5.8 range up to 5.13, with the largest group in the 5.12s. Several of the so-called sport lines are run out enough that a piece or two of gear is welcome, so expect them to feel serious for their grade. Most visitors stick to the fifteen or so best-known bolted lines.
ct_sport_routes.parking_note: Leave the car at the Crescent Lake Park lot in Southington; the trail to the cliff starts from there.

ct_gay_city_split_rock.blurb: A small knot of boulders on a hillside in Gay City State Park, Connecticut, close to the Split Rock trail. You get a couple of climbable faces, comfortable top-outs and flat landings, which makes it a friendly spot for newer boulderers. Of the 18 problems, most sit between V0 and V4, with a handful of harder lines reaching V6 to V10. The rock is only a minute or so from the trail, so a short session is easy to fit in. It is limited in size, so treat it as a local stop rather than a destination. Check yourself for ticks afterwards.
